hero.subtitle: The routing protocol that holds the Internet together

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
BGP-4 is the de facto standard exterior gateway protocol of the Internet. It enables autonomous systems (ASes) to exchange reachability information for IP prefixes, forming the global Internet routing table.

BGP is fundamentally a policy-based routing protocol. Unlike IGPs that optimize for shortest path, BGP allows network operators to implement complex routing policies based on business relationships, peering agreements, and traffic engineering goals.

BGP uses TCP (port 179) as its transport, ensuring reliable delivery of routing updates. The protocol is incremental - after the initial exchange of the full routing table, only changes are propagated.

sections.title: Protocol Overview
sections.content:
BGP is a path-vector protocol. Each route advertisement carries the complete AS path it has traversed, enabling loop detection and policy-based route selection.

OPENEstablishes BGP session, exchanges capabilities
UPDATEAdvertises new routes or withdraws previously announced routes
KEEPALIVEMaintains session liveness (sent every 60 seconds by default)
NOTIFICATIONReports errors and terminates the session

sections.title: Path Attributes
sections.content:
Each BGP UPDATE message carries a set of path attributes that describe the properties of the advertised routes. These attributes drive the route selection process.

AS_PATHOrdered list of ASes the route has traversed (loop detection)Well-known mandatory
NEXT_HOPIP address of the next-hop router for the advertised prefixWell-known mandatory
LOCAL_PREFPreference value within an AS (higher = preferred)Well-known discretionary
MEDMulti-Exit Discriminator - suggests preferred entry point (lower = preferred)Optional non-transitive
COMMUNITYTags for implementing routing policies (e.g., no-export)Optional transitive
ORIGINOrigin of the route: IGP, EGP, or IncompleteWell-known mandatory

sections.title: Decision Process
sections.content:
When multiple paths exist to the same destination, BGP uses a well-defined decision process to select the best path. Attributes are compared in strict order of priority.

1. Highest LOCAL_PREF
Prefer routes with the highest local preference value (iBGP only).
2. Shortest AS_PATH
Prefer routes that traverse the fewest autonomous systems.
3. Lowest ORIGIN
Prefer IGP over EGP over Incomplete origin types.
4. Lowest MED
Prefer the path with the lowest multi-exit discriminator (same neighbor AS).
5. eBGP over iBGP
Prefer externally learned routes over internally learned ones.
6. Lowest IGP Cost
Prefer the path with the lowest IGP metric to the next hop (hot potato routing).

sections.title: UPDATE Message
sections.content:
The UPDATE message is the core of BGP routing information exchange. Each message can simultaneously withdraw previously advertised routes and advertise new ones.

BGP UPDATE Message
+-----------------------------------------------------+
|   Withdrawn Routes Length (2 octets)                |
+-----------------------------------------------------+
|   Withdrawn Routes (variable)                       |
+-----------------------------------------------------+
|   Total Path Attribute Length (2 octets)             |
+-----------------------------------------------------+
|   Path Attributes (variable)                        |
+-----------------------------------------------------+
|   Network Layer Reachability Information (variable)  |
+-----------------------------------------------------+

NLRI (Network Layer Reachability Information) encodes IP prefixes using a length-prefix pair, allowing efficient representation of routes ranging from /0 (default) to /32 (host routes).

sections.title: Finite State Machine
sections.content:
The BGP Finite State Machine (FSM) defines the lifecycle of a BGP session, from initial connection to established state and error handling.

IdleInitial state; no connection attempt in progress
ConnectTCP connection in progress to the peer
ActiveListening for TCP connection from the peer
OpenSentOPEN message sent; awaiting peer OPEN
OpenConfirmOPEN received; awaiting KEEPALIVE
EstablishedSession is up; UPDATE messages can be exchanged

A BGP session stuck in the Active state usually indicates a connectivity problem or misconfiguration. This is one of the most common troubleshooting scenarios in BGP operations.
